questions.stem: Which part of an animal cell controls the cell's activities and contains the genetic material?
options: Nucleus
Cell membrane
Cytoplasm
Mitochondria
questions.hint: Think of the cell's "control centre".
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — It holds the chromosomes (DNA), which carry the instructions for everything the cell does.
B: Incorrect — This controls what goes in and out of the cell, not the cell's activities.
C: Incorrect — This is the jelly where most chemical reactions happen. It doesn't hold the genetic material.
D: Incorrect — These release energy by aerobic respiration. They don't control the cell.

questions.stem: In which part of a cell does aerobic respiration take place?
options: Ribosomes
Mitochondria
Cell wall
Nucleus
questions.hint: This part is often called the "powerhouse" of the cell.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Ribosomes make proteins. They don't carry out respiration.
B: Correct — Aerobic respiration happens here, releasing energy for the cell.
C: Incorrect — The cell wall strengthens plant cells. No reactions for energy happen there.
D: Incorrect — The nucleus holds the genetic material and controls the cell.

questions.stem: What is the function of ribosomes?
options: Storing cell sap
Photosynthesis
Protein synthesis (making proteins)
Controlling what enters and leaves the cell
questions.hint: They are tiny, and found in every type of cell, even bacteria.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Cell sap is stored in the permanent vacuole of plant cells.
B: Incorrect — Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts.
C: Correct — Ribosomes join amino acids together to build proteins.
D: Incorrect — That is the job of the cell membrane.

questions.stem: Which structure is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
options: Mitochondria
Chloroplast
Nucleus
Cell membrane
questions.hint: Which part captures light?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Both plant and animal cells respire, so both have mitochondria.
B: Correct — Chloroplasts absorb light for photosynthesis. Animal cells don't photosynthesise, so they don't have them.
C: Incorrect — Both plant and animal cells have a nucleus.
D: Incorrect — Both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane.

questions.stem: What is the cell wall of a plant cell made of?
options: Starch
Cellulose
Glucose
Protein
questions.hint: It is a tough carbohydrate that makes up plant fibres.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Starch is a carbohydrate plants use to store energy, not to build cell walls.
B: Correct — Cellulose fibres make the cell wall strong, which supports the cell.
C: Incorrect — Glucose is a sugar made in photosynthesis. Plants turn some of it into cellulose, but the wall itself is cellulose.
D: Incorrect — Plant cell walls aren't made of protein.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes a prokaryotic cell, such as a bacterium?
options: It is much larger than a eukaryotic cell
It contains chloroplasts
Its genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus
It has a nucleus and mitochondria
questions.hint: "Pro" cells are simpler than eukaryotic cells.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Prokaryotic cells are much smaller, roughly 10 to 100 times.
B: Incorrect — Bacteria don't have chloroplasts. Chloroplasts are found in plant cells.
C: Correct — Bacteria have a single loop of DNA floating in the cytoplasm, plus small rings called plasmids.
D: Incorrect — These are features of eukaryotic cells (plants, animals, fungi).

questions.stem: What are plasmids?
options: Rings of DNA inside the nucleus of plant cells
Organelles that release energy in plant cells
Structures that make proteins
Small rings of DNA found in bacteria
questions.hint: They are extra DNA found in bacteria.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Bacteria don't have a nucleus, and plasmids aren't found in plant nuclei.
B: Incorrect — That describes mitochondria.
C: Incorrect — That is what ribosomes do.
D: Correct — Plasmids are small extra rings of DNA in the cytoplasm of prokaryotic cells.

questions.stem: A bacterium is 2 µm long. An animal cell is 20 µm across. How many times bigger is the animal cell?
options: 100 times
10 times
18 times
40 times
questions.hint: Divide the bigger size by the smaller size.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That would need the animal cell to be 200 µm.
B: Correct — 20 ÷ 2 = 10. That is one order of magnitude bigger.
C: Incorrect — 18 is the difference (20 − 2). "How many times bigger" means divide, not subtract.
D: Incorrect — 40 is 20 × 2. You need to divide, not multiply.

questions.stem: Why does a sperm cell contain lots of mitochondria?
options: To release energy for the tail to swim
To give the cell a strong wall
To make food by photosynthesis
To store the father's genetic material
questions.hint: What does a sperm cell need to do to reach the egg?
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, which releases the energy the tail needs to move.
B: Incorrect — Mitochondria don't make walls, and animal cells have no cell wall.
C: Incorrect — Sperm cells are animal cells and can't photosynthesise.
D: Incorrect — The genetic material is in the nucleus in the head of the sperm.

questions.stem: How is a root hair cell adapted to its job?
options: It has many ribosomes to digest the soil
It has a very thick cell wall to protect it from soil
It has many chloroplasts to photosynthesise underground
It has a long projection that gives a large surface area
questions.hint: Its job is absorbing water and minerals from the soil.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Ribosomes make proteins. Root hair cells don't digest soil.
B: Incorrect — A thick wall would slow down absorption. That is the opposite of what it needs.
C: Incorrect — There is no light underground, so root hair cells have no chloroplasts.
D: Correct — More surface touching the soil means water and mineral ions are absorbed faster.

questions.stem: Under a microscope, a cell's image is 6 mm wide. The real cell is 0.02 mm wide. What is the magnification?
questions.hint: Magnification = image size ÷ real size.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — 6 ÷ 0.02 = 300.
B: Incorrect — Too big by 10 times. Check the decimal place: 6 ÷ 0.02 = 300.
C: Incorrect — Check the division: 6 ÷ 0.02 = 300.
D: Incorrect — This multiplies the two sizes. You need image size ÷ real size.

questions.stem: Why can scientists see ribosomes with an electron microscope but not with a light microscope?
options: Electron microscopes have a much higher magnification and resolution
Electron microscopes show cells in colour
Electron microscopes can look at living cells
Ribosomes only exist in cells prepared for electron microscopes
questions.hint: Think about how much detail each microscope can show.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Higher resolution means two points very close together can be seen as separate, so tiny structures like ribosomes become visible.
B: Incorrect — Electron microscope images are black and white. Colour is added afterwards.
C: Incorrect — The specimens must be dead. This is a disadvantage of electron microscopes.
D: Incorrect — Ribosomes are in all cells. They are just too small for a light microscope to show.

questions.stem: A light microscope has a magnification of × 400. The image of a cell is 10 mm long. What is the real length of the cell?
options: 4 µm
250 µm
2.5 µm
25 µm
questions.hint: Real size = image size ÷ magnification. Then convert mm to µm (1 mm = 1000 µm).
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This divides the magnification by the image size (400 ÷ 10 ÷ 10). The formula is image ÷ magnification.
B: Incorrect — Too big by 10 times. 10 ÷ 400 = 0.025 mm = 25 µm.
C: Incorrect — The decimal place has slipped. 0.025 mm is 25 µm, not 2.5 µm.
D: Correct — 10 ÷ 400 = 0.025 mm. 0.025 × 1000 = 25 µm.

questions.stem: Which statement about cell differentiation is correct?
options: Differentiated cells can easily change into any other type of cell
Most plant cells differentiate early on, but many animal cells can differentiate throughout life
Most animal cells differentiate early on, but many plant cells can differentiate throughout life
Animal and plant cells both stop differentiating at birth
questions.hint: Think about which can regrow from a cutting: a plant or a person?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Once a cell has specialised, it usually can't change into another type.
B: Incorrect — This is the wrong way round.
C: Correct — That is why you can grow a whole new plant from a cutting, but an adult human can't regrow a lost arm.
D: Incorrect — Plants keep growing new specialised cells at their meristems all their lives.

questions.stem: In school labs, bacteria cultures are usually incubated at a maximum of 25 °C. Why?
options: To kill any bacteria that might be harmful
To reduce the chance of growing bacteria that could cause disease in humans
Because 25 °C is the temperature at which all bacteria grow fastest
Because the agar jelly melts above 25 °C
questions.hint: Which bacteria grow best at human body temperature?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — 25 °C doesn't kill bacteria. It is a warm temperature where many bacteria can still grow.
B: Correct — Human pathogens grow best near body temperature (37 °C). Keeping it at 25 °C makes them much less likely to grow.
C: Incorrect — Many bacteria grow faster at higher temperatures. 25 °C is chosen for safety.
D: Incorrect — Agar stays solid well above 37 °C. It only melts at very high temperatures.

questions.stem: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting with one bacterium, how many will there be after 2 hours?
questions.hint: Work out how many times it divides, then double that many times.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — 2 hours = 120 minutes. 120 ÷ 20 = 6 divisions. 2⁶ = 64.
B: Incorrect — This doubles the number of divisions (6 × 2). The population doubles each time, so it's 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2.
C: Incorrect — 32 is 2⁵, which is only 5 divisions. 120 ÷ 20 = 6 divisions.
D: Incorrect — 6 is the number of divisions, not the number of bacteria.

questions.stem: Where are chromosomes found in an animal cell?
options: In the cell membrane
In the cytoplasm
In the nucleus
In the ribosomes
questions.hint: They carry the genetic material.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The membrane controls what enters and leaves. It doesn't hold chromosomes.
B: Incorrect — In animal cells, chromosomes are kept inside the nucleus, not loose in the cytoplasm.
C: Correct — Chromosomes are found in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells.
D: Incorrect — Ribosomes make proteins. They don't contain chromosomes.

questions.stem: How many chromosomes are in a normal human body cell?
questions.hint: Chromosomes come in pairs, and humans have 23 pairs.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — 92 would be double the normal number.
B: Correct — 23 pairs = 46 chromosomes.
C: Incorrect — 44 is two short. Don't forget the pair of sex chromosomes.
D: Incorrect — 23 is the number of pairs. Sex cells (eggs and sperm) have 23, but body cells have 46.

questions.stem: What is a chromosome made of?
options: Cell membrane
Glucose and starch
A DNA molecule that carries many genes
A single gene
questions.hint: It is a long, coiled molecule that carries genes.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The membrane surrounds the cell. It isn't part of a chromosome.
B: Incorrect — These are carbohydrates. They don't carry genetic information.
C: Correct — Each chromosome is one long DNA molecule with a large number of genes along it.
D: Incorrect — A chromosome carries many genes, not just one.

questions.stem: What does mitosis produce?
options: Four genetically different cells
Two genetically different cells
One larger cell
Two genetically identical cells
questions.hint: Mitosis is used for growth and repair, so the new cells must be copies.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That describes meiosis, which makes sex cells.
B: Incorrect — Mitosis makes identical cells, not different ones.
C: Incorrect — Mitosis splits one cell into two. It doesn't join cells together.
D: Correct — Mitosis makes two daughter cells with exactly the same chromosomes as the parent cell.

questions.stem: What happens in the first stage of the cell cycle, before mitosis?
options: The cytoplasm and cell membrane divide
The cell joins with another cell
One set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell
The cell grows, copies its DNA and makes more ribosomes and mitochondria
questions.hint: The cell gets ready to split into two.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is the final stage, which forms two cells.
B: Incorrect — Cells don't join together in the cell cycle.
C: Incorrect — This happens during mitosis, the second stage.
D: Correct — The cell needs two full sets of everything, one for each new cell.

questions.stem: Why is cell division by mitosis important in multicellular organisms?
options: To make sex cells (gametes)
To create genetic variation
To release energy from glucose
For growth and repair
questions.hint: What happens when you cut your skin?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Gametes are made by meiosis, not mitosis.
B: Incorrect — Mitosis makes identical cells, so it doesn't create variation.
C: Incorrect — That is respiration, not cell division.
D: Correct — Mitosis makes new identical cells, so the body can grow and replace damaged cells.

questions.stem: During mitosis, what happens to the chromosomes?
options: The chromosomes are destroyed
The number of chromosomes is halved
One set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell
The chromosomes join with chromosomes from another cell
questions.hint: Each new cell needs a full set.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The chromosomes are kept. The new cells need them.
B: Incorrect — Halving happens in meiosis, not mitosis.
C: Correct — So each new cell gets a full, identical set of chromosomes.
D: Incorrect — That happens at fertilisation, not mitosis.

questions.stem: What happens in the final stage of the cell cycle?
options: The cell grows bigger
The DNA is copied
The cytoplasm and cell membranes divide to form two identical cells
Chromosomes are pulled to each end of the cell
questions.hint: This stage finishes the split.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Growth happens in the first stage.
B: Incorrect — DNA is copied in the first stage, before mitosis.
C: Correct — This completes the cell cycle.
D: Incorrect — This is mitosis, the stage before.

questions.stem: What is a stem cell?
options: A specialised cell found only in plant stems
A cell that has lost its nucleus
A cell that can only make more cells of exactly its own type
An undifferentiated cell that can make more cells and turn into other types of cell
questions.hint: It hasn't "chosen a job" yet.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Stem cells are found in animals and plants. The name has nothing to do with plant stems.
B: Incorrect — Stem cells have a nucleus. They need their DNA to divide.
C: Incorrect — Stem cells can differentiate into other types too.
D: Correct — Stem cells aren't specialised yet, so they can divide and become different cell types.

questions.stem: Where are stem cells found in plants?
options: Xylem
Meristems
Guard cells
Root hair cells
questions.hint: These areas are at the tips of roots and shoots, where the plant grows.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Xylem is specialised tissue that carries water.
B: Correct — Meristem tissue can differentiate into any type of plant cell, all through the plant's life.
C: Incorrect — Guard cells are specialised to open and close stomata.
D: Incorrect — Root hair cells are already specialised to absorb water.

questions.stem: How do embryonic stem cells differ from adult bone marrow stem cells?
options: There is no difference between them
Embryonic stem cells can't divide
Adult bone marrow stem cells can turn into any type of cell; embryonic ones can't
Embryonic stem cells can turn into most types of human cell; adult bone marrow stem cells can only form some types, such as blood cells
questions.hint: Which is younger and less specialised?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Embryonic stem cells can form many more types of cell.
B: Incorrect — Embryonic stem cells divide very easily.
C: Incorrect — This is the wrong way round.
D: Correct — That is why embryonic stem cells could be used to treat more conditions.

questions.stem: In therapeutic cloning, an embryo is made with the same genes as the patient. Why is this useful?
options: Stem cells from the embryo are not rejected by the patient's body
It can cure every genetic disease
It means there are no ethical objections
The stem cells grow faster than normal cells
questions.hint: Think about what the immune system does to cells it doesn't recognise.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The cells have the patient's own genes, so the immune system treats them as "self".
B: Incorrect — It isn't a cure for everything. Research is still going on.
C: Incorrect — Many people still object, because an embryo is used and then destroyed.
D: Incorrect — Matching genes is about avoiding rejection, not speed.

questions.stem: Which is a risk of using stem cells in medical treatment?
options: Transfer of a viral infection to the patient
The stem cells always cause the patient to die
The stem cells can't divide once inside the patient
The patient's DNA is permanently changed into the donor's
questions.hint: Cells grown in a lab could carry something harmful.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — If the stem cells are infected with a virus, the patient could catch it.
B: Incorrect — This is not true. Bone marrow transplants already save lives.
C: Incorrect — The worry is more about cells dividing out of control, not failing to divide.
D: Incorrect — A treatment doesn't replace all of the patient's DNA.

questions.stem: A human body cell (46 chromosomes) divides by mitosis, and then both new cells divide by mitosis again. How many cells are there, and how many chromosomes does each have?
options: 2 cells, each with 46 chromosomes
4 cells, each with 92 chromosomes
4 cells, each with 23 chromosomes
4 cells, each with 46 chromosomes
questions.hint: Mitosis doubles the number of cells but keeps the chromosome number the same.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is after only one division. There were two rounds.
B: Incorrect — DNA is copied before division, but each new cell still ends up with 46.
C: Incorrect — Halving to 23 only happens in meiosis.
D: Correct — 1 → 2 → 4 cells. Mitosis keeps the full set of 46 in every cell.

questions.stem: Why do plant growers use meristem tissue to make clones?
options: To make large numbers of identical plants with useful features quickly and cheaply
To increase genetic variation in the crop
To make plants that don't need light
Because meristem cells can't divide
questions.hint: Think about speed and getting exactly the plant you want.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — For example, disease-resistant crops, or saving rare species from extinction.
B: Incorrect — Clones are identical, so there is no variation. That is actually a risk if a new disease appears.
C: Incorrect — Cloned plants still need light for photosynthesis.
D: Incorrect — Meristem cells divide very easily. That is why they are used.

questions.stem: What is diffusion?
options: The movement of water through a partially permeable membrane
The movement of particles from a lower concentration to a higher concentration
The movement of particles using energy from respiration
The net movement of particles from a higher concentration to a lower concentration
questions.hint: Particles spread out from where there are lots of them.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That describes osmosis, a special type of diffusion.
B: Incorrect — That is active transport, which needs energy.
C: Incorrect — Diffusion is passive. It doesn't need energy.
D: Correct — Particles spread out down a concentration gradient. No energy is needed.

questions.stem: Which gas diffuses from the air in the lungs into the blood?
options: Nitrogen
Water vapour
Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
questions.hint: Your cells need this gas for aerobic respiration.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Nitrogen isn't taken up by the body. It's breathed out unchanged.
B: Incorrect — Water vapour is breathed out, not absorbed for respiration.
C: Correct — There is more oxygen in the air in the lungs than in the blood, so it diffuses into the blood.
D: Incorrect — Carbon dioxide diffuses the other way, from the blood into the lungs, to be breathed out.

questions.stem: What is osmosis?
options: The movement of water from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
The movement of water from a concentrated solution to a more dilute solution
The movement of salt particles across a membrane
The movement of water using energy from respiration
questions.hint: It is only about water.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Water moves to where there is less water, and more solute.
B: Incorrect — This is the wrong way round.
C: Incorrect — Osmosis is the movement of water, not solutes.
D: Incorrect — Osmosis is passive. It doesn't need energy.

questions.stem: What does active transport need that diffusion does not?
options: Sunlight
Energy from respiration
Nothing, they are the same process
Water
questions.hint: It moves substances "uphill".
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Sunlight is needed for photosynthesis, not active transport.
B: Correct — Moving substances against a concentration gradient takes energy.
C: Incorrect — They are different. Diffusion goes down a gradient for free; active transport goes up it using energy.
D: Incorrect — Active transport moves dissolved substances, but water isn't what makes it different from diffusion.

questions.stem: Which change would increase the rate of diffusion?
options: A smaller surface area
A bigger difference in concentration
A thicker membrane
A lower temperature
questions.hint: Think: difference in concentration, temperature, surface area.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Less surface means fewer particles can cross at once.
B: Correct — A steeper concentration gradient means faster diffusion.
C: Incorrect — Particles have further to travel, so diffusion is slower.
D: Incorrect — Particles move more slowly when it's colder, so diffusion slows down.

questions.stem: Urea is a waste product made in cells. Where does it diffuse to?
options: From the blood into the cells
From the cells into the stomach
From the cells into the blood plasma, to be removed by the kidneys
From the cells into the lungs to be breathed out
questions.hint: It needs to get to the kidneys.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is the wrong way. Cells make urea, so their concentration is higher.
B: Incorrect — Urea is carried in the blood to the kidneys, not the stomach.
C: Correct — There is more urea in the cells than in the plasma, so it diffuses into the blood.
D: Incorrect — Urea is removed in urine, not breathed out.

questions.stem: Root hair cells take in mineral ions by active transport. Why can't they use diffusion?
options: Root hair cells don't have a cell membrane
The concentration of mineral ions in the soil is usually lower than inside the root
Mineral ions are too big to move at all
The concentration of mineral ions in the soil is usually higher than inside the root
questions.hint: Compare the amount of minerals in the soil with the amount inside the root.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — All cells have a cell membrane.
B: Correct — To move ions from low to high concentration, the cell must use energy.
C: Incorrect — They do move. They just need energy to go against the gradient.
D: Incorrect — If that were true, diffusion would work. The soil is usually more dilute.

questions.stem: After a meal, sugar is absorbed from the gut into the blood even when the blood has more sugar than the gut. How?
options: By diffusion
By osmosis
By photosynthesis
By active transport
questions.hint: Moving against a gradient needs energy.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Diffusion can only move sugar from a higher to a lower concentration.
B: Incorrect — Osmosis only moves water.
C: Incorrect — Photosynthesis is how plants make glucose. It doesn't move it.
D: Correct — Active transport uses energy from respiration to move sugar into the blood against the concentration gradient.

questions.stem: A piece of potato is left in a very concentrated salt solution. What happens to its mass?
options: It decreases, because water leaves the potato cells by osmosis
It increases, because salt enters the potato by osmosis
It increases, because water enters the potato cells by osmosis
It stays the same, because potatoes don't do osmosis
questions.hint: Which side has more water, the potato cells or the salty solution?
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The solution is more concentrated, so water moves out of the cells.
B: Incorrect — Osmosis is the movement of water, not salt.
C: Incorrect — Water would enter if the solution were more dilute than the cells, like pure water.
D: Incorrect — Potato cells have partially permeable membranes, so osmosis happens.

questions.stem: Why doesn't a single-celled organism, like an amoeba, need special exchange surfaces?
options: It has a large surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion through its membrane is fast enough
It doesn't need oxygen or food
It uses osmosis to get oxygen
It has a small surface area to volume ratio
questions.hint: Think about surface area compared with volume.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Substances only have a short distance to travel, so diffusion meets its needs.
B: Incorrect — All living organisms need to exchange substances.
C: Incorrect — Osmosis only moves water. Oxygen enters by diffusion.
D: Incorrect — Small organisms have a large ratio, not a small one.

questions.stem: A 1 cm cube has a surface area to volume ratio of 6 : 1. What is the ratio for a 2 cm cube?
questions.hint: Surface area = 6 × (side × side). Volume = side × side × side.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Surface area = 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 cm². Volume = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³. 24 : 8 = 3 : 1.
B: Incorrect — The ratio changes as the cube gets bigger. Bigger objects have a smaller ratio.
C: Incorrect — This is upside down. The ratio is surface area : volume = 24 : 8.
D: Incorrect — The ratio gets smaller as the cube gets bigger, not larger.

questions.stem: In the osmosis practical, a potato cylinder goes from 2.00 g to 2.30 g. What is the percentage change in mass?
questions.hint: % change = (change ÷ starting mass) × 100.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This divides by the final mass (2.30). Always divide by the starting mass.
B: Incorrect — The mass went up, so the change is positive.
C: Correct — Change = 0.30 g. 0.30 ÷ 2.00 × 100 = 15%. It gained mass, so it's +15%.
D: Incorrect — This uses 0.30 as if it were the percentage. You must divide by the starting mass.

questions.stem: In the osmosis practical, potato pieces in 0.3 mol/dm³ sugar solution don't change mass. What does this tell you?
options: No water molecules move at all
The potato cells are dead
The solution inside the potato cells has about the same concentration as 0.3 mol/dm³
The sugar has entered the potato cells
questions.hint: No change in mass means no net movement of water.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Water still moves both ways. It just balances out.
B: Incorrect — Osmosis happens across the membrane whether or not the result shows a change.
C: Correct — Water moves in and out at the same rate, so there is no net movement.
D: Incorrect — The cell membrane stops sugar moving in this practical. Only water moves.

questions.stem: Which feature would make an exchange surface, like the lungs or fish gills, LESS effective?
options: A large surface area
A thick lining
Being ventilated
A good blood supply
questions.hint: Good exchange surfaces are big, thin and well supplied with blood.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — A large surface area makes exchange faster.
B: Correct — A thick lining increases the distance particles must travel, so diffusion is slower.
C: Incorrect — Ventilation brings in fresh air or water, keeping the gradient steep.
D: Incorrect — Blood carries substances away, keeping the concentration gradient steep.

questions.stem: A red blood cell and a plant cell are both put in pure water. The red blood cell bursts but the plant cell doesn't. Why?
options: Plant cells don't take in water by osmosis
Water leaves the red blood cell, making it burst
The red blood cell has a cell wall that splits
Water enters both cells by osmosis, but the plant cell has a cell wall that stops it bursting
questions.hint: Which cell has extra support around it?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — They do, which is why the plant cell swells and becomes firm.
B: Incorrect — Water enters the red blood cell. Losing water would make it shrink.
C: Incorrect — Animal cells, including red blood cells, have no cell wall.
D: Correct — The strong cellulose wall pushes back, so the plant cell just becomes firm (turgid).
